Classroom window, third seat from the left. She traces condensation down the glass while the cicadas outside fill the empty room with summer.
Afternoon light cuts across deserted desks in long gold bars. She hasn't moved in twenty minutes. The chalkboard still says Tuesday.
The classroom smells like eraser dust and heat. She presses her forehead to the window glass and watches a single cloud cross the schoolyard.
Last period ended an hour ago. She sits on the windowsill with her shoes off, watching the shadow of the school creep across the yard.
Empty classroom, blue curtains drifting inward. She holds a pencil she forgot to use, looking at the shimmer rising from the asphalt below.
Under the kotatsu, she wraps both hands around her mug. The cat shifts its weight on the blanket above her knees. Outside, snow is already ankle-deep.
She's been reading the same page for ten minutes. The cat purrs. The radiator clicks. The window holds a perfect square of grey-white winter sky.
Green tea gone lukewarm. She doesn't reheat it. The cat sleeps on the kotatsu surface above her feet, one paw hanging off the edge.
Snow ticks softly against the glass. She pulls the kotatsu blanket tighter and listens to it, cup pressed against her collarbone, eyes half-closed.
The mandarin orange she meant to eat sits on the kotatsu corner. The cat has relocated it slightly with one deliberate paw. She doesn't notice.
Rooftop, 1am. She lies on her back with a half-empty vending-machine coffee, watching Orion inch westward over the Shinjuku glow on the horizon.
She found the Big Dipper twenty minutes ago and hasn't moved since. The city hums below. The can in her hand is cold now.
The Tokyo skyline smears orange-pink against low clouds to the south. She sits cross-legged on the rooftop, chin on her knees, a star above her head.
Cassiopeia, faint through the light pollution. She traces it with one finger held up against the sky, breath clouding in the October air.
She brought a blanket up here. It smells like the cedar chest in the hallway. Above her, a satellite crosses silently between two bright stars.
The convenience store at 2am has no other customers. The worker folds an empty box. Outside, rain makes halos around every streetlight on the block.
She buys onigiri and canned peach tea. He gives her the receipt without looking up. The rain outside makes the windows completely opaque.
He's refolding magazines that don't need refolding. She stands at the hot-food case, steaming, watching the rain through the glass door.
Fluorescent hum, rain on the roof, the distant clunk of the drink machine cycling. They haven't spoken. The clock says 2:17am.
She counts out exact change very slowly. He waits. Neither of them seems in any hurry to return to whatever they came from tonight.
6:03am train. She's the only one in the car. Pink light spreads low across flooded paddies outside, the sky turning from lavender to pale gold.
She falls asleep against the window and wakes to full sunrise streaking the glass. Her stop is next. She watches the light anyway.
The train passes through a tunnel and comes out the other side into sudden blinding pink dawn. She squints. She doesn't look away.
Her breath fogs the train window glass. Outside, a farmer is already in his field, a dark shape in the orange-pink morning mist.
Half the seats are empty. The fluorescents haven't switched off yet against the risen sun. She watches the light change colors on the seat fabric.
Her bicycle shadow is long and golden on the paddy-field road. She's not pedaling hard. The satchel bumps against her back with each gentle push.
Frog sounds from the paddies on both sides. She freewheels downhill with her arms out, uniform ribbon snapping back, no one watching.
The rice paddies hold the afternoon sky flat and perfect beside the road. She passes through her own reflection without noticing.
Gravel road, warm asphalt smell, a crow on the fence post. Her shadow stretches twenty meters behind her toward where school used to be.
She stops pedaling and lets the bike drift to a slow halt in the middle of the road. Nothing is coming either way. She just looks at the light.
The umbrella is red and the puddles are lavender. She steps around each one carefully, watching the sky fold into the water beneath her feet.
Rain-smell, wet shoe-leather, the sound of water pouring from a drainpipe down a wall. She walks slowly. There's nowhere she needs to be fast.
Her sock is wet from a puddle she miscalculated. She keeps walking. The twilight turns the rain silver and then briefly, deeply purple.
A car passes and sends a sheet of gutter water into the air beside her. The umbrella takes most of it. She laughs once, quiet.
She stops at the crosswalk and watches the streetlights come on one by one down the avenue in the rain. The walk signal blinks red.
The summer festival ended an hour ago. A single paper lantern still burns outside the closed shrine gate, and someone dropped a red flower beneath it.
Empty street, paper cups rolling in the faint wind, the smell of yakitori still faint in the warm air. One lantern. Nothing else lit.
She finds the spot where they stood at the festival and the ground is scuffed and the lantern above her is still swaying, barely.
The sheets billow out from the balcony line in the blue-hour wind. She watches them from her chair, hands around nothing, city just audible below.
She hung laundry an hour ago and hasn't gone back inside. The sheets go pink, then grey-blue, then white under the streetlights.
Blue hour on the balcony. A pillowcase lifts and falls in a slow breath of wind. Somewhere below, a train sounds its departure chime.
Steam rises in a slow curl from the bowl. The ramen chef refills the tea without being asked. The stool beside her is empty. Outside, midnight.
The only sound is the stock simmering and the rain and the occasional turn of a page. She eats slowly. There is no reason to hurry anything.
Noodle shop, 11:45pm. She stares into the broth, watching the oil rings drift. The chef watches the rain. The noodles go soft. She doesn't mind.
Platform three. One figure stays on the concrete, one appears in the window. The train chime sounds. Neither of them waves first.
She watches the train diminish down the track until it's just two red lights, then one, then just the dark and the sound of the rails cooling.
Rooftop, noon, bento open on her lap. She eats slowly and watches a cumulus cloud rebuild itself above the gymnasium, enormous and unhurried.
Old neighborhood, dusk. A calico sits on the stone wall between two houses and watches her pass with eyes that hold the last of the amber light.
Vending machine alley, 3am. She stands in front of it for a long time, lit orange-warm from below, hand raised and still, not yet deciding.
Under the sakura alone. Petals collect in the corners of her open book. She stopped reading. The pale light through the blossoms is enough.
Classroom window, fourth row. She watches a dragonfly hover above the emptied schoolyard, motionless in the thick August air, wings catching the last gold.
The eraser dust still hasn't settled. She sits sideways in her chair, legs over the armrest, watching heat rise visibly off the gymnasium roof.
Summer detention, but no teacher came. She sits alone counting ceiling tiles while the fan oscillates slowly, lifting the corner of someone's forgotten homework.
Afternoon light has moved all the way across the floor since she sat down. The chalkboard says Wednesday. She thinks it might be Thursday now.
She breathes on the window and draws a small circle in the fog, then watches it disappear before she can decide what to put inside it.
The kotatsu orange sits half-peeled in a bowl. She fell asleep on her textbook. The cat has moved from the table surface to her shoulder.
Snow falling in heavy curtains past the glass. She watches it bury the garden slowly, both hands wrapped around the mug, forgetting to drink.
The cat steps deliberately across her open textbook, pauses, sits directly on the most important diagram. She lets it. Outside, everything is white.
She refills the mug with hot water and slides back under the kotatsu blanket until only her head shows. The room fills with the smell of barley tea.
3pm and already dark enough for the lamp. She turns it on and the kotatsu and the cat become a small warm country entirely separate from winter.
She brought her phone up to the rooftop but hasn't looked at it. Venus is setting behind the apartment block to the west, slow and deliberate.
She can name four constellations and is trying to remember a fifth. The city glow makes it harder. She keeps looking anyway, neck tilted all the way back.
The rooftop door is propped open with a cinder block. Faint television sounds drift up from the fourth floor. Above her, Scorpius rises over Shibuya.
She watches a plane cross overhead, too slow for a satellite, blinking red and white. Below it, the whole city hums its single continuous note.
October rooftop, 11pm. She's wrapped a hoodie around her knees. The moon is three days past full and casts shadows from the water-tower she didn't notice before.
2am. He restocks the drink cooler one can at a time. She reads the same magazine back-cover standing up. Rain fills every pause between them.
The receipt prints longer than seems necessary for one rice ball. She folds it carefully into her pocket. Outside, the rain has changed to something quieter.
He's arranged the three remaining hot-food items into a neat line in the warmer. She watches him do it. Neither of them questions being here now.
She reads the nutritional label on a canned coffee for four full minutes. He dims the front signage slightly against the 3am regulations. Rain continues.
Both of them look at the door when a bicycle passes slowly outside through the rain, rider hunched, light wobbling. Neither says anything. The clock ticks.
Dawn train, no announcements. She watches snow powder blowing sideways across a frozen paddy outside, the sky still purple at its lowest edge.
The train car sways gently around a long curve. Through the window, a single lit farmhouse in the dark fields, smoke rising straight in cold air.
She watches her reflection in the black window glass overlap with the slowly brightening landscape behind it, both images uncertain, both briefly real.
A heron stands in the flooded field just outside the window as the train passes. It doesn't move. She turns to watch it go until it's gone.
Pink light crosses the vinyl seat in front of her and climbs the ceiling slowly as the train turns east. She tracks it without moving her head.
She crests the low bridge on her bicycle and below, the paddies mirror the whole slow sky. She stops pedaling and lets the moment carry her down.
Her satchel swings wide on the curve. A heron lifts from the irrigation ditch beside her and she watches it all the way until it's just white and gone.
Late afternoon, long shadows from the cedar windbreak striping the road gold and dark alternately. She rides through them one by one like counting.
She's singing something quietly to herself, not quite loud enough to hear. The paddy road is empty both directions. Her shadow is enormously long behind her.
Cicada sound so thick it has texture. She stops the bicycle at the crossroads and stands with one foot down, listening to where it's loudest.
She steps deliberately into a wide shallow puddle and stands still in it, watching the ripples reach the curb before she walks on through the rain.
The umbrella handle is damp from her grip. She tilts it back to look straight up at the grey-pink twilight through the stretched nylon above her face.
Rain gathers at the gutter edge and falls in one clean sheet to the street beside her. She watches it close enough to feel the mist. Keeps walking.
The streetlight above her flickers twice and holds. In the puddle at her feet, it flickers too, twice, reflected perfectly. She steps around it gently.
She slows at the gate of the house with the flooded stone garden. In the rain, the garden is a different place entirely. She stands looking a long time.
A single red lantern at the shrine entrance, wick still drawing down. Beneath it on the gravel path, a dropped yukata sash, pale blue, slowly dampening.
Festival night gone quiet. The yakisoba cart is locked and sheeted. One unlit lantern spins slowly on its string above the empty stone path.
She walks the festival grounds after closing, paper cups and a forgotten goldfish bag dried flat on the stone. Above the gate, one lantern holds on.
Balcony, blue hour. The sheet she hung has gone from warm white to soft grey. She reaches out and takes the corner in both hands, holds it a moment.
She stands at the balcony rail and watches the city's last light leave the windows of the tower across the road, floor by floor, slowly going out.
The pillowcase is almost dry. She unpins it and holds it against her face, breathing in the day-smell. Below, someone locks a bicycle, distant, small.
Ramen at midnight. She lifts the soft-boiled egg half on her chopstick and studies it briefly, like a small moon. Replaces it gently. Continues eating.
The chef refills the pickled ginger without her asking. She nods without looking up. The broth is still hot. Outside, the last bus passes without stopping.
Counter seat, end stool. She watches steam rise and drift rightward in the extraction vent's pull, a slow consistent lean, like weather in miniature.
Two figures, platform end. The green light comes on. One of them exhales and the breath shows white in the cold air between them, briefly, then nothing.
She puts one hand flat on the train door after it closes. It's warm from the car interior for just a moment, then the train takes the warmth with it.
School rooftop, bento half-eaten. She lies on her back and watches the cloud she was tracking dissolve completely before she can name what it resembled.
Evening street, the cat on the stone wall narrows its eyes once and looks away first. She stops anyway and they share a moment of mutual disregard.
3am vending machine. She selects the one she always gets, then cancels it, then stands still again in the amber warmth. The alley waits around her.
Under the sakura, very still. A petal lands on the back of her hand. She watches it, not moving, until the next small wind takes it somewhere further.
Classroom window, late August. She's drawn a small sun in the corner of the glass fog and is watching it slowly erase itself in the heat.
Empty classroom, third floor. The curtain lifts once in a breath of hot air and settles. She keeps her eyes on the flagpole. Nothing is moving.
She's been here since the bell. The janitor passes in the hall without looking in. She presses one palm flat to the warm glass and counts the windows across the yard.
The afternoon has gone gold and then amber without her deciding anything. She closes her notebook without opening it. The cicadas know something she doesn't.
She found a pencil someone left on the sill. She rolls it back and forth under her palm. Outside the schoolyard empties itself slowly, bicycle by bicycle.
The cat is a still warm weight across her shins. She stopped reading an hour ago. The snow outside has buried the garden chair entirely since morning.
She pours the last of the pot and it fills the cup only halfway. She drinks the half cup. The cat adjusts. Outside, the snow recomposes itself in the wind.
Kotatsu warmth, winter silence. She draws her knees up and the blanket tent closes around her. The cat above shifts its weight like a small slow tide.
Her textbook is open to a diagram she has looked at without seeing for thirty minutes. The snow light comes through flat and even. The cat breathes audibly.
She peels the mandarin one slow segment at a time and sets each piece on the kotatsu corner. The cat sniffs one. Outside, snow erases the garden incrementally.
She climbed up here to think about something specific and has thought about nothing instead. The city orange sits low on every cloud to the south.
Jupiter, she thinks. Or a plane. She waits. It doesn't blink and doesn't move. She decides: Jupiter. Stays another hour.
She can feel the cold of the rooftop concrete through the blanket now. Somewhere over Ikebukuro, a star she hasn't named yet holds very steady.
The can is empty but she doesn't move to throw it away. Perseus is rising over the apartment block. She watches with both hands wrapped around nothing.
She climbs up here most Fridays. She's told no one. The city below makes its sound. Above it, the stars make their older, quieter one.
2am, rain on the canopy. He lines the sandwich shelf quietly with new stock. She stands in the back aisle holding a hand warmer she hasn't paid for yet.
She buys warm corn soup and stands at the window to drink it. He goes back to inventory. Outside, the rain pushes a receipt across the wet asphalt.
He's mopping the same square meter very slowly. She reads every word on the chip bag she's already decided not to buy. Rain. Clock. Rain.
The fluorescent above the register has a slight flicker neither of them has mentioned. She watches it from the magazine aisle. He watches the door. Rain continues.
She asks for chopsticks she doesn't need. He counts them out carefully, two pairs. Outside, the rain finds new angles against the glass door.
5:54am. The train is almost empty. The platform lights still look like night. Outside, one thin band of colour at the horizon holds everything it has.
The landscape outside the window is flat and gradually revealed, field by frozen field, like someone showing her a secret they're not sure about yet.
She watches her reflection in the dawn window become slowly transparent as the light rises outside, the world replacing her face with rice paddies.
Her bag is on the seat beside her. She has moved it three times to let no one in particular sit down. The sunrise reaches the seat fabric and she leaves it.
The train leans through a long morning curve. Every window fills with the same pale pink simultaneously. She watches it happen like a slow communal decision.
She takes the long paddy-field road by choice. It adds twelve minutes. She has never once arrived late. The math of this pleases her quietly.
A kite circles above the far dike, riding something invisible. She tracks it from the bike without turning her head, pedaling slow, satchel swaying.
The road narrows between two paddies and the sky doubles below her on both sides. She rides between two skies, small and unhurried and entirely alone.
Evening, paddy road. Her uniform ribbon has come loose and she hasn't fixed it. The light coming low from the west makes her shadow very specific.
She reaches the crest where the fields open south all the way to the hills. Every time. She still stops every time. The bike ticks to a halt on its own.
Rain, homeward. She counts puddles by size. The largest one holds half the street and a complete cloud she didn't notice overhead until the water showed her.
Her umbrella has a small tear she traces with her fingertip while she waits at the crossing. The twilight comes in between pink and old copper.
The rain smell changes block by block, pavement to garden wall to the dry-paper scent near the bookshop that's already closed. She slows to catch it.
She lets the umbrella down to her shoulder and tilts her face up once. Two seconds of rain, eyes closed. Then the umbrella back up. She keeps walking.
Puddle at the shrine gate holds the torii upside down, perfect and wavering. She steps over it sideways rather than through it. The rain doesn't notice.
The goldfish bags on the empty game counter are deflated and dry in their plastic. One lantern outside the closed gate spins two slow degrees in the warm air.
She left early but walked back alone an hour later. The festival grounds smell like burned sugar and river. Above the gate, one lantern still has opinions.
Paper cups, a lost sandal, the sound of the generator still winding down somewhere behind the closed shrine fence. The lantern light finds the sandal.
Evening on the balcony. The sheet nearest the railing is completely dry but she's left it hanging to watch it move. It moves. That's enough for now.
She leans on the rail and watches one lit window across the courtyard. Someone's silhouette passes behind it once, then the curtain draws. Blue hour completes itself.
The pillowcase carries a smell of the day in it when she unpins it, warm and faint. She holds it a moment in both arms before folding. The city below continues.
Midnight ramen, end seat. She wraps both hands around the bowl rim and breathes the steam in. The chef scores a block of chashu in silence. Both of them patient.
She eats the noodles in long slow pulls and watches the chef's reflection in the steel above the stove, moving quietly through a task that has no urgency.
11pm noodle counter, one other customer asleep on their arms at the far end. She eats. The soup fills its own quiet. The rain fills the rest.
Platform eight, 9pm. The second figure doesn't board immediately. The door stays open an extra moment. Neither of them fills it with anything lasting.
She stands where the last car stopped long after the train has gone. The platform clock advances. She watches it make one full minute before she moves.
Rooftop noon, cumulus building to the east. She eats her tamagoyaki and watches the cloud climb thirty meters between bites. It has somewhere to be.
She closes the bento lid and lies back on the rooftop and lets a cloud replace her thoughts. It does this readily, slowly, without being asked.
Old neighborhood stone wall, a tabby tracks her with slow head-rotation as she passes below. At the corner it loses interest before she does.
Late afternoon in the bookshop, no other customers. She reads the first page of eight different books and replaces each one carefully. Dust drifts through one clean bar of light.
Apartment floor, evening rain. She lies on her side with the book held above her face. The rain on the glass becomes a sound she stops distinguishing from quiet.
Classroom window, second row. She's stopped pretending to study. The gymn roof shimmers below with stored heat, and a single dragonfly holds perfectly still in August.
The chalkboard says Friday in faded chalk. She sits backward in her chair, arms folded on the seatback, chin resting there, watching the light migrate across the floor tiles.
Last club member left twenty minutes ago. She sits on the far windowsill with her socks on the radiator, watching the shadow of the flagpole lengthen toward the gate.
She found someone's forgotten ruler on the sill. She balances it on one finger and watches the schoolyard empty itself, bus by bus, into the thick summer afternoon.
Afternoon has gone completely amber. She holds her pencil case in both hands without opening it, watching heat-shimmer rise off the bicycle shed roof below the window.
The kotatsu has been on since October. She slides in until her chin nearly rests on the surface, both hands around the cup, listening to the snow accumulate its silence.
She woke from a textbook nap to find the room dark and the cat relocated to her lap. The snow outside the window has doubled since she fell asleep.
Winter afternoon, lamp already on. She and the cat have reached a territorial compromise: blanket to her waist, all surfaces above the knee belonging to him.
The barley tea cools and she doesn't notice. The cat tucks both paws under its chest and becomes a loaf. Outside the window, snow buries the potted plant by degrees.
She's been watching the snow since the cat settled. It falls in curtains, then diagonals, then straight down. The mug is empty. She refills it without looking away.
Rooftop, 2am. She sits with her back against the water tower, watching the Pleiades clear the apartment block to the northeast, one bright cluster arriving without announcement.
She brought two cans up and has drunk neither. Below her the city makes its orange ceiling. Above it, Vega holds the southwest quarter alone and very clear.
October, rooftop, legs pulled to chest. The moon is behind her. She watches its light fill the street below without seeing the source, just the effect, quiet and silver.
She can see three distinct weather systems from up here: clear south, clouded west, something moving in from the bay. Above all of it, Jupiter refuses to flicker.
Midnight rooftop, the can warm in her hands from the machine. The Milky Way is almost invisible through the city glow, but almost is enough to keep her looking.
2am. She's the third customer tonight. He folds the receipt before she asks for it. Outside, rain divides itself evenly between the awning and the bicycle stand.
The hot-food warmer holds two items at this hour. She studies them equally without choosing. He restocks the onigiri shelf one careful row at a time. Rain. Hum. Rain.
She pays in exact coins counted into her palm beforehand. He receives them without comment. The rain outside turns the window into a slow abstract painting. Neither looks at it.
He turns the shop playlist off at 2am. She doesn't notice for several minutes, then does, and the silence between them becomes a different kind of company.
She asks where the umbrellas are. He points. She looks. She already has one. Neither of them addresses this. The rain approves. The clock advances to 2:31.
5:47am train, two other passengers asleep in separate cars. She watches the sky transition from indigo to rose-gray above the frozen paddies, the colours not yet committed to anything.
She pressed her forehead to the cold window glass and the sunrise met her there, pink through the condensation ring her breath made, personal and enormous and brief.
The train emerges from the mountain cut into full dawn light. Every window ignites simultaneously. The one sleeping passenger doesn't wake. She watches on behalf of everyone.
Her station is four stops. She watches a egret stand motionless in a flooded field for the entire second stop interval, regal and indifferent to the train's passage.
Pale gold spreads from the horizon inward, filling the flat landscape below its own reflection in the paddies. She watches both versions, the one above and the one below.
Afternoon, paddy-field road. She found a feather on the asphalt and tucked it into her satchel flap. It trembles there as she pedals, pointing the direction she's already going.
The irrigation gate is open and water crosses the road in a thin bright sheet. She lifts her feet and rolls through it and the cold hits her ankles like a small fact.
Late afternoon, paddy-field crossroads. She brakes and puts one foot down and eats the last of her lunch bread standing over the handlebars. The herons don't look up.
Her chain skips on the uphill and she half-stands on the pedals to push through it. The paddies stretch flat on both sides. The sky does the same. She keeps going.
She's been riding slowly enough that a dragonfly has paced her for thirty seconds. She doesn't speed up. The afternoon has all the room it needs.
The umbrella is inside out briefly at the corner and she rights it laughing once, quietly, while the rain falls sideways into the lamplight around her.
She walks through her own reflection in every puddle, fractured and reassembled, a different version of herself in each one, all of them heading home.
Twilight rain, homeward. She slows at the old wall with the wisteria because the wet smell of it is different from every other smell on the street and she wants it again.
The rain lightens for one block near the temple and she lowers the umbrella and walks in it openly, face lifted, before it picks up again at the crossing.
Her shoes are soaked. She's past caring about this and into something else, a different relationship to the rain, more honest, less defended. She walks accordingly.
The shrine lantern had been burning since dusk. She passes the empty grounds at midnight: paper cups against the fence, the smell of sparklers still faint, the lantern faithful.
Empty festival path, her sandals on stone. A single goldfish swims in its bag on the gravel where someone set it down and didn't come back. The lantern above it burns.
The mikoshi has gone back inside the shrine. The crowd has dissolved into the city. She stands where the dancing was and one lantern measures out the last of the evening.
Blue hour, balcony. The futon cover she hung at noon has gone from white to the specific grey-blue of distance. She touches its edge with two fingers on her way back inside, then stops.
She leans over the balcony rail and watches the laundry below on the next floor: someone else's ordinary life suspended on a line, swaying, intimate and entirely indifferent to her.
The last shirt on the line is her father's. She unpins it and holds it against herself briefly in the cooling air before folding it. Below, the city settles into its evening register.
Ramen counter, 11pm. She holds the chopsticks without separating them, watching the chashu soften further in the broth. The chef doesn't rush her. The soup holds the room.
She eats the bamboo shoot last because she likes it least and wants to end on something else. The chef notices without meaning to. Outside, taxis accumulate at the corner.
11:30pm, last customer. She asks for extra menma. He adds it without measuring. The rain outside has been the same rain for three hours. She's begun to feel it's hers.
The departure chime sounds. One figure in the window, one on the platform, both performing the expression people wear when words have already said everything they're going to.
She boards and finds the window seat facing back. She watches the platform until the bend takes it. He was still standing there. She keeps watching the bend.
Rooftop, 12:08pm. Her bento has a note inside from her mother about a dentist appointment. She folds it carefully and watches a cloud dismantle itself above the gymnasium.
She eats her tamagoyaki and watches the pigeons negotiate the gymnasium roof below with the specific urgency of creatures who have decided everything matters very much.
Evening, old neighborhood. The stone wall cat has been there every Thursday for four months. She stops to tell it this. It regards the middle distance. The light goes amber.
